question: What is the \(100\)th digit to the right of the decimal point in the decimal form of \(\dfrac{4}{37}?\)
solution:
Use long division until a remainder repeats, because the same remainder will produce the same later digits. Starting with remainder \(4\), multiply each remainder by \(10\) to obtain the next decimal digit:
\[
\begin{aligned}
40&=37\times1+3,\\
30&=37\times0+30,\\
300&=37\times8+4.
\end{aligned}
\]
The digits produced are \(1,0,8\), and the final remainder is the original \(4\). Thus these steps repeat forever, giving
\[
\frac4{37}=0.\overline{108}.
\]
Each block has three digits. Since \(99=33\times3\), the first \(99\) digits form \(33\) complete blocks. The \(100\)th digit is the first digit of the next block, namely \(1\), choice B.

edges.reason: A one-based index offset is reduced modulo the block length once the block and any prefix have been verified. Deriving and indexing a rational decimal expansion is distinct from the inverse decimal-to-fraction conversion. Formal modular indexing is a route component; long division with ordinary remainders also locates the block.
edges.scope: Reduce the requested decimal position modulo the repetend length.

edges.reason: Aligning an infinite repeating tail uses exact decimal shifts, not finite rounding. Place-value shifts and the requested reduced-fraction condition are shared. edges.scope: place-value change under multiplication by powers of ten
